title: Specimen Identification: Label the Right Sample for the Right Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A correctly collected specimen is useless if it is mislabeled. Use required patient identifiers and label specimens according to policy at the point of collection.
recognize: Unlabeled, pre-labeled, mismatched, or uncertain-source specimens can cause wrong-patient diagnosis or treatment.
priorities: Verify patient identity before collection and match labels/orders to the patient and specimen source.
assessMonitor: Check identifiers, source, date/time, collection requirements, and transport conditions.
interventions: If specimen identity is uncertain, stop and follow the rejection/recollection process rather than guessing.
medicationSafety: Wrong-patient laboratory results can trigger inappropriate medication changes; protect identity before testing begins.
teaching: Explain why repeated identity checks are a safety measure, not unnecessary duplication.
delegationScope: Collection may be assigned within competency; the collector is responsible for correct identification and labeling under policy.
examTrap: Fixing a label from memory after leaving the bedside.
oneLinePearl: If you cannot prove whose specimen it is, do not make the result prove anything.

title: Blood Cultures: Contamination Creates False Infection
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Blood-culture accuracy depends heavily on aseptic collection, adequate volume, correct identification, and timely transport. Contamination can trigger unnecessary antibiotics and hospitalization.
recognize: Improper skin preparation, bottle-septum contamination, inadequate volume, and single-set collection can reduce diagnostic reliability.
priorities: Use patient identifiers, appropriate skin/bottle disinfection, correct volume, and multiple sets per institutional protocol when ordered.
assessMonitor: Document collection site, method, date/time, collector, and transport.
interventions: Collect before antimicrobial therapy when possible without delaying urgent treatment of an unstable patient.
medicationSafety: Do not delay indicated sepsis antibiotics solely to obtain an ideal specimen sequence when the patient is unstable.
teaching: Explain that more than one set may be needed to distinguish bloodstream infection from contamination.
delegationScope: Collection authority follows competency and facility policy; interpretation remains with the clinical team.
examTrap: Repeating a culture only after antibiotics because collection technique was rushed despite a stable patient.
oneLinePearl: Clean collection protects both diagnosis and stewardship.
sourceBasis: CDC Prevent Adult Blood Culture Contamination guidance updated 2026-03-31

title: Timed Drug Levels: The Clock Is Part of the Specimen
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A drug level drawn at the wrong time can be clinically misleading. Verify whether the ordered level is trough, peak, random, or otherwise time-linked before collection.
recognize: A mislabeled collection time can make an apparently high or low concentration uninterpretable.
priorities: Confirm last dose time, next dose time, and required collection window before drawing.
assessMonitor: Record exact collection time and relevant dose timing.
interventions: If timing is wrong or uncertain, notify the team rather than presenting the result as valid.
medicationSafety: Do not hold, repeat, or change dosing independently based on an incorrectly timed level.
redFlags: Dose given before required trough without clarification
teaching: Patients should report when they last took the medication if outpatient levels are being checked.
delegationScope: Collection may be assigned; timing verification and abnormal-result escalation require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Calling any pre-dose result a trough without verifying timing.
oneLinePearl: For timed levels, time is part of the lab value.

title: Point-of-Care Glucose: Treat the Patient, Verify the Meter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Point-of-care glucose is fast but not infallible. An implausible result or a symptomatic patient whose presentation does not fit the number requires repeat/confirmatory evaluation without delaying emergency treatment for obvious hypoglycemia.
recognize: Poor perfusion, contamination on fingers, device/QC problems, and strip issues can distort results.
priorities: Use correct technique and assess symptoms alongside the number.
assessMonitor: Check meter QC/status, sample site, perfusion, symptoms, medication timing, and repeat/confirmatory testing as indicated.
interventions: Treat severe symptomatic hypoglycemia per protocol while obtaining confirmation if needed.
medicationSafety: Do not administer a large insulin correction from an implausible point-of-care result without verification.
teaching: At home, wash/dry hands and recheck unexpected readings before making nonemergency dose decisions according to the diabetes plan.
delegationScope: Testing may be delegated to trained personnel; interpretation and treatment decisions require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Believing the meter over the symptomatic patient without rechecking.
oneLinePearl: Fast data still needs clinical context.
sourceBasis: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Coagulation Specimens: Collection Error Can Mimic Bleeding Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Coagulation results are vulnerable to collection problems such as wrong tube fill, contamination from heparinized lines, and labeling/timing errors. Question implausible results before making medication conclusions.
recognize: A sharply abnormal result that conflicts with the patient's trend or clinical status may reflect collection error.
priorities: Follow tube, fill, mixing, and line-draw requirements exactly.
assessMonitor: Review anticoagulants, collection site, timing, and previous results.
interventions: Escalate suspected contaminated or invalid specimens for recollection per policy.
medicationSafety: Do not independently change anticoagulant dosing from a suspect specimen.
teaching: Patients should report anticoagulants and dose timing when relevant.
delegationScope: Collection follows competency; medication decisions remain with authorized clinicians.
examTrap: Treating an unexpected extreme result as true without reviewing how the specimen was collected.
oneLinePearl: Before acting on a coagulation result, trust the specimen first.

title: Urine Culture Collection: Reduce Contamination Before Calling It Infection
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Urine-culture technique should match the collection method and clinical question. Contamination can lead to unnecessary antibiotics, especially when nonspecific symptoms are over-attributed to bacteriuria.
recognize: Poor clean-catch technique, collection from a drainage bag, or delayed transport can compromise results.
priorities: Use the ordered clean-catch/catheter collection method and correct container/transport.
assessMonitor: Document symptoms, collection method, source, and timing.
interventions: For catheterized patients, obtain specimens from the designated sampling port using aseptic technique rather than the drainage bag.
medicationSafety: Do not equate asymptomatic bacteriuria with a need for antibiotics without the clinical team's assessment.
delegationScope: Collection may be delegated within competency; interpretation requires licensed/provider review.
examTrap: Collecting urine from the catheter drainage bag for culture.
oneLinePearl: A clean result starts with a clean collection.

title: Stool Testing: Match the Sample to the Question
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Stool testing requires the correct specimen, container, timing, and indication. Testing formed stool for some diarrheal pathogens or using contaminated specimens can mislead care.
recognize: Active diarrhea, blood/mucus, antibiotic exposure, travel, immune status, and outbreak context change the diagnostic question.
priorities: Verify the ordered test and specimen requirements before collection.
assessMonitor: Record stool appearance/frequency, isolation status, recent antibiotics, and collection time.
interventions: Avoid urine/water contamination and transport according to laboratory requirements.
medicationSafety: Do not suppress severe infectious diarrhea reflexively with antimotility medication before clinical review.
teaching: Explain collection steps clearly when patients collect the specimen themselves.
delegationScope: Collection may be delegated; deterioration and infection-control implications require licensed oversight.
examTrap: Sending any stool sample without checking whether it meets the test's requirements.
oneLinePearl: Right test, right stool, right timing.

title: Critical Laboratory Result: Read Back, Act, and Close the Loop
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A critical result is a communication emergency. Verify the result/read-back process, assess the patient, notify the responsible clinician per policy, and document the closed-loop response.
recognize: Critical potassium, glucose, hemoglobin, INR, blood gas, or other values can signal immediate physiologic risk depending on context.
priorities: Confirm patient/result, assess the patient, and escalate promptly using the facility critical-result pathway.
assessMonitor: Trend symptoms, ECG/vitals when indicated, relevant medications, and repeat testing/orders.
interventions: Use read-back/closed-loop communication and document who was notified and what action followed.
medicationSafety: Do not administer high-risk corrective treatment outside protocol/order simply because a critical value is reported.
teaching: Explain urgent repeat testing/treatment as appropriate.
delegationScope: Critical-result escalation is a licensed responsibility even if the specimen collection was delegated.
examTrap: Documenting the result and assuming someone else will notice it.
oneLinePearl: Critical data is not complete until the communication loop closes.

title: Diagnostic Test Preparation: Verify the Prep Before the Test
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Fasting, medication holds, hydration, contrast/allergy considerations, and timing requirements vary by test. Verify the actual preparation instructions rather than relying on memory or a generic 'NPO' rule.
recognize: Incorrect preparation can produce invalid results or create avoidable medication/dehydration risk.
priorities: Check the ordered test's current preparation requirements and relevant comorbidities/medications.
assessMonitor: Verify last oral intake, medication timing, renal status when relevant, allergies, pregnancy status when indicated, and consent/procedure readiness.
medicationSafety: Never hold chronic medications automatically because a patient is NPO; follow test-specific orders/protocols.
teaching: Provide specific written preparation instructions and teach-back.
delegationScope: Reinforcement may be delegated within role; initial/complex preparation teaching and medication decisions follow licensed/provider authority.
examTrap: Withholding every morning medication because the patient is NPO.

title: Hemolyzed Specimen: Recollect Before Treating the Artifact
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Hemolysis can falsely alter analytes such as potassium and compromise interpretation. When the laboratory flags a specimen and the result is inconsistent with the patient, recollection may be safer than treating an artifact.
recognize: Difficult draws, forceful transfer, small needles, prolonged tourniquet use, or specimen handling problems can increase hemolysis risk.
priorities: Review the laboratory flag, patient condition, and urgency before acting on a suspect value.
assessMonitor: Compare with prior results, ECG/symptoms when relevant, collection method, and repeat specimen.
interventions: Recollect using proper technique when ordered/indicated and promptly escalate true symptomatic abnormalities.
medicationSafety: Do not administer potassium-lowering treatment solely for a likely hemolyzed potassium without clinical confirmation unless an emergency clinician directs otherwise.
teaching: Explain why a blood test sometimes must be repeated.
delegationScope: Collection may be assigned; interpretation of flagged results requires licensed oversight.
examTrap: Treating the number before checking whether the sample itself is trustworthy.
oneLinePearl: Question the specimen before correcting the artifact.
